analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: A bill to open the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain to oil drilling drew 131 cosponsors, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 1980 law that bans drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and require the Interior Department to hold competitive lease sales for oil and gas there, with the first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months. It layers on environmental conditions, gives half the drilling revenue to the State of Alaska, and directs most of the rest to an alternative-energy trust fund. It also shortens and narrows the environmental review process and limits court challenges to a single federal appeals court.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain access to federal lands that have been closed to drilling since 1980, buying leases at competitive bids and paying at least a 12.5% royalty on production. The State of Alaska would receive 50% of bonus, rental, and royalty revenue, and local communities on the North Slope would be eligible for impact aid of up to $11 million. Alaska Native corporations would receive cleared title to land entitlements, and leasing terms would require employment efforts for Alaska Natives and project labor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies; Alaska state and local governments

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act of 1980, the provision that prohibits oil and gas leasing and development on the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain, and declares drilling there compatible with the refuge's purposes [S3].

Requires the Interior Secretary to run competitive lease sales by sealed cash-bonus bids, with the first sale offering at least 200,000 acres of the tracts with the greatest hydrocarbon potential, and sets expedited deadlines of 15 months for regulations and 22 months for the first sale [S3].

Splits 50% of bonus, rental, and royalty revenue to the State of Alaska and sends most of the remainder to a newly created ANWR Alternative Energy Trust Fund to fund programs under the 2005 and 2007 energy laws [S3].

Creates a Coastal Plain Local Government Impact Aid Assistance Fund, capped at $11 million, to help the North Slope Borough, Kaktovik, and other affected Alaska communities pay for police, fire, water, medical, and mitigation services [S3].

Includes lease conditions such as a minimum 12.5% royalty, a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for fish and wildlife, a 2,000-acre cap on the surface footprint of production facilities, seasonal limits on exploration, reclamation liability for lessees, a ban on exporting oil produced under the leases, and a requirement that lessees negotiate project labor agreements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public owns the coastal plain and its oil; once opened, the resource is developed by private leaseholders under standard federal terms. Wildlife, habitat, and Alaska Native subsistence users would bear the environmental risk of industrial activity in a refuge, and the bill's own safeguards are partly self-eliminating: it deems drilling compatible with refuge purposes without further findings, deems a 1987 environmental statement sufficient for pre-leasing, forbids analyzing a no-leasing alternative, and allows only 20 days for public comments and only the D.C. Court of Appeals to hear challenges. Anyone arguing prices or revenues would rise for consumers is relying on the bill's title, not anything in the text.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, wildlife, and subsistence communities

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the legal barrier Congress created in 1980 and pre-clears its own review: it deems a 1987 environmental impact statement sufficient, forbids the Secretary from studying a no-leasing alternative, limits public comments to 20 days on a single preferred action, and restricts all court challenges to the D.C. Court of Appeals with the Secretary's analysis presumed correct [S3].

Environmental review and protections, while extensive on paper, are administered under a compressed schedule and a weakened judicial check, so the actual level of protection depends on the Interior Secretary in office rather than on enforceable outside review [S3].

The bill's name promises 'price reduction,' but the text contains no analysis or mechanism connecting drilling in the refuge to lower consumer prices; any price effect is speculative, while the main guaranteed effect is transferring access to publicly owned oil to private leaseholders [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a major giveaway of access to publicly owned oil with genuine mitigations: Alaska revenue sharing, local impact aid, an alternative-energy trust fund, Native hiring and contracting preferences, project labor agreements, and an export ban. But the environmental protections are largely in the hands of a Secretary on a 15-22 month clock, and the bill explicitly narrows environmental analysis and court review to make leasing litigation-proof. On balance, the main beneficiary is the oil industry, and the main irreversible cost falls on a wildlife refuge and the communities that depend on it.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on the first day of the 112th Congress, it was referred to three committees and then to subcommittees, and sat there without a markup or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on January 5, 2011 [S1].
131 House members cosponsored it, 125 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S4].

It was referred to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees on the day of introduction, and in the following weeks to subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources, Environment and the Economy, and Energy and Environment [S5].
No further action is recorded: no committee reported the bill, no vote was taken in either chamber, and it died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the oil industry gained no new access to the coastal plain, and the people and organizations that wanted the Arctic Refuge kept closed to drilling were better off. The State of Alaska and North Slope communities gained nothing either, since the revenue-sharing and impact-aid provisions died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of keeping the Arctic Refuge closed to drilling

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 125 of the 131 cosponsors were Republicans, with 6 Democrats joining, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is opening a federal wildlife refuge that has been closed to drilling since 1980 to competitive leasing by oil and gas companies. The industry's gain is access to publicly owned oil; the public shares in it only through the standard 12.5% royalty and Alaska's 50% revenue share, while bearing the environmental and subsistence costs.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and North Slope local governments
industries.note: Alaska would get 50% of lease revenues, and affected communities would get impact aid capped at $11 million for schools, police, water, and mitigation. These benefits exist only if drilling proceeds, so they ride on the same industrial activity that environmental and subsistence interests oppose.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation, Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill requires conveyance of surface and subsurface estates to settle long-standing land entitlements, requires leaseholders to use best efforts to hire and contract with Alaska Natives, and requires consultation with Kaktovik and the North Slope Borough on special areas. These are concrete local gains, though they are tied to development in the refuge that other Alaska Native subsistence users may oppose.
